newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND ESCAPES KILLY SHADOW WITH WORLD CUP WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND ESCAPES KILLY SHADOW WITH WORLD CUP WIN.

text.p: France's Luc Alphand completed the circle at the World Cup Finals, ending his most glorious season where he began his career and realising his dreams as one of the young "Top Guns" by becoming tops in Alpine skiing.
Most significantly to Alphand, the 31-year-old speed racer was finally able to rise above the shadow cast by French ski legend Jean-Claude Killy.
Alphand entered a new name into the record books, a new feat in the history of the World Cup and a new chapter for French skiing excellence on Sunday by winning the overall title.
"There is lots of emotion," said the relieved racer after his triumph, taken, ironically, at a standstill as he watched rival Kjetil Andre Aamodt fall short in the climactic slalom.
"It's like a liberation just now. The last two weeks have been very hard. There has been great pressure."
Alphand, who competed in his first World Cup race in the neighbouring Rocky Mountain resort of Aspen, capped a brilliant career by becoming the first speed specialist ever to win the overall title.

"Sometimes there has been too much weight for me. I'm only myself," said Alphand. "Sometimes it's hard enough to race. There is so much pressure from all the country with all the people behind me. But I'm very happy leading French skiing to a better place."
It had been 29 years since a Frenchman had claimed the most coveted ski championship. Feats of the great Killy cast an uncomfortable shadow over French skiers that followed.

"I'm really happy to change his name," said Alphand about adding a new championship entry to the honour roll. "Not for the way you might think. But after 30 years it was time for French skiing to replace something and put a new name there."
Alphand said he respected Killy but that his exploits became something of a burden on the young French skiers.

"When he won I was three years old," he said, dismissing the suggestion that Killy might have been an inspiration. "Oh, I heard his name for sure. For 10, 15 years on the team you always heard about Killy from the French media."
Killy dominated the very first season of World Cup, winning all three discipline titles and sweeping all five downhills in 1967. He repeated as overall champion again in 1968.

"But now the ski world is different. There are so many races, so many countries. But he has made an example. Not only in his sport life but also his after-career life. He is a big name in France. Not just in skiing but in life. "
Alphand's life in World Cup skiing was anything but easy.
He began as a would-be all-rounder, a member of an up-and-coming gang of French skiers known as the Top Guns along with Denis Rey, Franck Piccard and Jean Luc Cretier.
Towards the end of the 1980s, Alphand decided to concentrate on speed racing.
"When I first focused on downhill, I was a crash pilot," said the mountain man from Serre-Chevalier. "I went full speed ahead and knew all the hospitals near all the courses. I was so wild."
Injuries took their toll.

In 1987, he injured both hips and his thigh. In 1988, he hurt his ankle. His back, wrist and shoulder were damaged in 1989. The next year, he hurt a wrist and ankle. In 1992 he tore a pelvis muscle. A year later he tore ligaments in his knee.
"Finally, I learned to relax on my skis," says Alphand, a slightly-built man with a dashing goatee.
His big breakthrough came in January 1995 in Kitzbuehel. Alphand won his first downhill at that classic course and three hours later won his second downhill.
That began a flood of success that carried Alphand to the season's downhill title. He made it three downhill titles in a row this season and added the Super-G crown for good measure.
Now that Alphand has reached the peak, the end may well be in sight.
"I began here in the States in 1984 in Aspen," said Alphand. "We are here in 1997. Thirteen years is enough."
